items.note: Claim A asserts that unprocessed red meat consumption has no association with incident stroke, whereas Claim B states that it is associated with an increased risk of stroke.

Claim A indicates that the risk reduction for myocardial infarction is similar regardless of alcohol intake level, whereas Claim B asserts a continuous, log-linear decrease in risk with higher alcohol consumption.

Claim A finds no significant overall association between alcohol consumption and incident stroke, whereas Claim B reports that higher alcohol consumption is linearly associated with an increased stroke risk.

Claim A asserts a J-shaped curvilinear dose-response relationship between alcohol consumption and stroke risk, whereas Claim B asserts a linear relationship where higher consumption is consistently associated with higher risk.

Claim A finds no association between unprocessed red meat intake and incident diabetes, whereas Claim B reports that higher intake of red meat is associated with an increased incidence of type 2 diabetes.
Claim A asserts that alcohol consumption lowers all-cause mortality risk, whereas Claim B states that higher-quality studies show no such reduction in mortality risk.

Claim A finds that alcohol consumption significantly reduces all-cause mortality risk, whereas Claim B finds no significant reduction in mortality risk after controlling for abstainer biases and study quality.

Claim A reports a significant increase in coronary heart disease risk associated with higher triglyceride levels, whereas Claim B finds no significant association after adjusting for conventional risk factors.

Claim A reports a statistically significant increased risk of coronary heart disease associated with higher triglyceride levels, whereas Claim B reports no significant association after adjusting for risk factors.
Claim A finds a significant positive association between triglyceride levels and coronary heart disease risk after adjustment, whereas Claim B finds no significant association.
